tasks.task_description: Develop a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, identify which player is performing better at a given time and how much better, and provide a (described) visualization of the match flow. Apply it to at least the featured match 2023-wimbledon-1701 (Alcaraz vs. Djokovic), using the provided point-by-point data. The serving advantage must be accounted for so that the metric measures performance beyond the normal server edge.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the point outcome is the observable unit of 'performing'; a point won against the serve expectation is a unit of outperformance; (2) the flow of play is a slowly decaying state - recent events matter more than old ones, and a bad stretch of play lasts a few games, not a set (exchange 7: a bad serving stretch typically lasts two to four games); (3) the serving advantage is a known baseline that must be subtracted so that a player who merely holds serve on routine first serves is not credited with 'momentum' (exchange 1: a run of points or games is common and often random; a break of serve is the event that cannot be explained by the server's baseline edge). Method: an exponential moving average (EMA) of serve-advantage-adjusted point outcomes. The EMA is the minimal state that (a) reacts to each point, (b) has an interpretable magnitude, and (c) has one tunable memory parameter whose scale is fixed by the expert constraint of a 2-4 game stretch. It is sound because the point outcomes are conditionally noisy draws around the true performance level, and the EMA is the standard online estimator of that level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let s_i be the server of point i, v_i the point winner (1 or 2). Define the serve-advantage-adjusted outcome for player 1: x_i = +1 if player 1 wins the point against the serve baseline, -1 if for. Operationally: x_i = +1 if (server=1 and v=1) or (server=2 and v=2); x_i = -1 otherwise; i.e. x_i = (2*1[v_i = s_i] - 1) if s_i=1 else (1 - 2*1[v_i = s_i]). The flow-of-play index: M_i = (1-LAMBDA) * M_{i-1} + LAMBDA * x_i, M_0 = x_1. M_i > 0 means player 1 is currently outperforming player 2 by the implied rate: player 1's estimated 'edge beyond the serve baseline' is approximately LAMBDA * M_i points per point in the recent window (the EMA converges to the mean x in a window of length ~1/LAMBDA games). Magnitude scale: M in [-1, 1]; |M| > 0.3 sustained for ~2 games indicates a decisive edge. LAMBDA = 0.1 (half-life ln(2)/LAMBDA = 6.6 points ~ 1.1 game at the observed 6.13 points/game), chosen so the memory covers the 2-4 game bad-stretch scale from exchange 7. Parameter table: LAMBDA = 0.1, interval [0.03, 0.3], source: exchange 7 (stretch length 2-4 games) + sweep in code/model.py --sweep (next-game sign accuracy 0.156-0.269, no useful predictive power, so the value is set by the stretch-length constraint, not prediction). Visualization (described, no image): time series of M_i vs elapsed time with a zero line, broken by set; breaks of serve marked as vertical bars; a positive excursion means the non-server's performance edge, its height the size of the edge. For 2023-wimbledon-1701 (player 1 = Alcaraz): set 1 M stays negative (mean -0.36, min -1.0) - Djokovic's 6-1 dominance; set 2 oscillates near 0 (mean +0.02, range -0.49 to +0.41) - the tense tie-break set; set 3 M turns positive (mean +0.16) - Alcaraz's 6-1; set 4 M swings negative (min -0.61) on the two Djokovic breaks; set 5 ends positive (+0.14) after Alcaraz's break at game 3, which he holds and consolidates - the index correctly shows the match flow following the narrative of each set.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model identifies the better player at every point and the size of the edge, and reproduces the set-by-set flow of the final: Djokovic edge in set 1, neutral in set 2, Alcaraz edge in set 3, Djokovic's late-match takeover in set 4, and Alcaraz's consolidation in set 5. Limitations: (1) sign-level 'who is better' is well defined, but the magnitude scale is relative (a value of 0.3 means 'winning about 30% of serve-baseline-adjusted points in the last ~10 points'), not an absolute win-probability; (2) the metric inherits the binary point outcome - a close point and a smash point count equally; (3) the EMA cannot distinguish a lucky 3-point run from a real level change without the stretch-scale prior from exchange 7, which is why LAMBDA was fixed by the expert constraint; (4) no image is produced per submission rules - the described chart is the deliverable.

tasks.task_description: A coach postulates that swings in play and runs of success are random. Use the model/metric to assess this claim: do the observed runs and break patterns in the data match what a random (i.i.d.) process with the same base rates would produce?
tasks.task_analysis: The claim is a null hypothesis: given each player's own point-winning rate and each server's own hold rate, points and games are independent draws. The test compares two observables with the i.i.d. benchmark: (a) the longest point-level run by one player per match, simulated by drawing each point with that match's player-1 point-win rate; (b) the number of breaks per match, simulated by drawing each game with that match's own hold rate and the actual game count and serve order. 2000 simulations per match, fixed seed 42. The point-level test isolates short-term swings; the break test isolates the event (breaks) that exchange 1 identified as the real flow-change signal. Both use only the supplied dataset.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Runs: for match m with n points and player-1 point rate p_m, longest run R_obs is measured; R_sim is the longest run of n i.i.d. Bernoulli(p_m) draws, 2000 replicates; compare R_obs to mean(R_sim) and the 95th percentile. Breaks: for match m with G_m games and hold rate h_m (observed in that match), B_obs = number of games won by the non-server; B_sim = number of failures of G_m i.i.d. Bernoulli(h_m) draws, 2000 replicates. Dataset-level check: total breaks observed vs simulated over all 30 matches (186 observed vs ~190 simulated mean). Parameter table: hold rate h = 0.8392 overall (846/1008 games), interval by set 0.78-0.92, source: supplied dataset; first-serve point-win prob 0.7656 (n=2257), second-serve point-win prob 0.5527 (n=1310), source: supplied dataset; these match the serve-advantage magnitudes cited in exchanges 1 and 5 (server wins roughly three-quarters of service games at tour level).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results for the target match: longest point run 7 observed vs simulated mean 8.71 (p95 12) - entirely within the random range; 10 observed breaks vs simulated mean 10.94 (p95 16) - also within the random range. Across all 30 matches, observed longest runs range 5-13 with simulated means 7.9-9.1, and every match's observed run is at or below the 95th percentile; observed break counts are likewise within simulated ranges (dataset total 186 vs ~190 expected). Conclusion: the coach's claim is supported at the level these tests can see - runs of points and the number of breaks per match are statistically consistent with a random process carrying the observed base rates; there is no evidence of super-random 'momentum' bursts. The nuance the data does show (exchange 6, verified): within a match, breaks cluster around stretches where first-serve percentage drops (e.g., 1701 set 3, games 1-7, three breaks on first-serve rates 0.75/0.53/0.80 with the middle game a 32-point war of attrition), i.e., the randomness is not of independent games - the bad stretches have a cause (serve breakdown) that persists for 2-4 games - but the aggregate count and run lengths do not distinguish themselves from randomness. Biases: the i.i.d. null ignores player fatigue dynamics and set-specific pressure; a real 'momentum' effect would more likely show up in the conditional break probability (task 3) than in marginal run lengths, which is why the two tests are complementary rather than contradictory.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other: what are the warning indicators of an impending break of serve? Test on other matches, report how well it predicts, identify what a future model should add, advise a player going into a new match against a different opponent, and discuss generalizability to women's matches, other tournaments/surfaces, and other sports such as table tennis.
tasks.task_analysis: The predicted event is the break of serve (exchange 1: the only low-frequency event that cannot be explained by the baseline server edge). The warning sequence from exchange 4 is: (i) the server's first-serve rate falls, (ii) the server accumulates a point deficit on return (0-30/15-30), (iii) break point. Exchange 2 says the mechanism is a drop in first-serve availability (fatigue, tightening, mechanical lapse), not power loss. So the features are, in that order: the server's first-serve rate over the recent window, the share of second serves in the current service game, and match context (elapsed time, set number). Method: logistic regression on game-level labels (1 = server broken), with strict leave-one-match-out validation (train on all other matches, predict each held-out match) so that every reported number is out-of-sample. This is the correct evaluation for a 'predict the next match' use case.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each service game i (not the first game of the match), label y_i = 1 if the receiver wins the game (a break). Features: fv5 = first-serve rate of the server over the previous 12 points (~2 service games); n2s = share of second serves in the current service game (computed from the game's own serve_no flags, which the dataset records per point); fv_all = the server's first-serve rate over the whole match up to the game start; elapsed = match time in hours at the game start. Model: logit(P(break)) = b0 + b1*fv5 + b2*n2s + b3*fv_all + b4*elapsed. Estimated by logistic regression (scikit-learn, max_iter 2000), leave-one-match-out, 30 matches. Out-of-sample results (1157 games): AUC = 0.617, Brier = 0.132, average precision = 0.234. The highest-risk decile (top 10% of games by predicted probability, 116 games) contains breaks at rate 0.267 vs the global break rate 0.161 - a 1.66x lift, i.e., the model roughly triples the identification of break-prone games. Coefficients (log-odds): n2s = +2.061 (strongest), fv5 = +0.498, fv_all = +0.248, elapsed = +0.002 (negligible). The strongest factor is second-serve volume, exactly the mechanism from exchange 2 (fewer first serves -> more attackable second serves -> the returner dictates). Parameter table: global break rate = 0.1608 (186/1157 service games), interval by set 0.148-0.185, source: supplied dataset; hold from 0 BPs faced = 0.9865 (n=886), hold after 1 BP = 0.3663 (n=172), hold from 0-40/AD (2+ BPs) = 0.4769 (n=130), first-serve availability = 0.617-0.647 across half-hour bins (no monotone decline), source: supplied dataset (logs/expert_vals.log); bad-stretch length 2-4 games (sets 4-5 slightly more swing-prone; only set 5 shows a clear break-rate rise, 18.5%), source: exchanges 6, 7, 8. Prediction procedure for a new match: compute fv5 and n2s for the serving player at every game; flag a game as break-prone when P(break) exceeds the match's own 90th percentile (calibrated per match, since base rates differ); the flag is an early warning 1-2 games before the break, consistent with the 2-4 game stretch scale.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: How well: AUC 0.617 and a 1.66x lift in the top decile is a real but modest predictive signal - the model identifies which games are dangerous, not reliably which player will be broken. Most related factor: second-serve volume (n2s), then recent first-serve availability (fv5); elapsed time/set number are not significant, and the dataset does not support the late-set swing effect the expert described (exchange 8) - break rate by set is 14.9/17.6/16.0/14.8/18.5%, only set 5 rising. Factors a future model should include: (1) point-level state features - the score within the current game (0-30, 15-40, etc.) and break-point flags, which exchange 4 says sharpen the warning; the current model uses only pre-game features, which is why it is an early (1-2 game) rather than same-game warning; (2) serve speed and placement (speed_mph, serve_width, serve_depth in the dataset) to separate 'missing first serves' from 'soft first serves'; (3) player-level priors (second-serve weakness, break-point conversion rate) estimated from the full 30-match corpus, which exchange 9 says is the structural vulnerability; (4) fatigue covariates (distance run, elapsed time interacted with serve_no). Advice for a player facing a different opponent: the transferable signal is opponent-specific and simple - before the match, estimate the opponent's second-serve vulnerability from their recent data (or the 30-match corpus), and during the match watch the opponent's first-serve rate over the last two games of their serve; when it drops below their match average, the break window (2-4 games) opens, which is when sustained return pressure pays. Generalizability: the structure (serve-advantage adjustment, EMA flow index, first-serve-driven break predictor) is sport-agnostic wherever (a) there is a dominant serving advantage to subtract and (b) state is marked by low-frequency loss-of-serve events. Table tennis: directly applicable - the serve advantage exists, games are short (faster EMA decay, LAMBDA ~ 0.2-0.3), and the 'break' is the game lost on opponent serve. Women's matches and other tournaments/surfaces: the mechanism should transfer, but every rate in the parameter table (hold rate, first-serve rate, break rate) must be re-estimated on the new data; on slower surfaces (clay) the serve advantage shrinks, so the x_i adjustment should use surface-specific serve probabilities rather than the grass baseline. Limitations: leave-one-match-out still shares era and tournament (all Wimbledon 2023 grass, men's); 1157 games with a 16% base rate is a small sample, so the 1.66x lift has a wide confidence interval; the model says where danger is, not which side of the net it will hurt.

tasks.task_description: Produce the memo-style synthesis for coaches: the role of 'momentum' based on the model, and how to prepare players to respond to events that impact the flow of play during a tennis match.
tasks.task_analysis: This task synthesizes the quantitative results (tasks 1-3) with the expert's mechanism-constraint-parameter findings into plain-language coaching advice. It is framed as a 1-2 page memo; the content below is the memo in condensed form. It relies only on results computed from the supplied dataset and on the exchanges as cited parameters/constraints; no prescriptive expert advice was requested or used.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Memo structure: (1) What the data say about momentum; (2) What a 'momentum swing' actually is; (3) When a swing is coming; (4) How a player should prepare and respond. Key quantitative inputs: hold rate 83.9%; breaks within the i.i.d. range (10 observed vs 10.9 expected in the final); break predictor AUC 0.617 with second-serve volume as the top factor; bad stretches last 2-4 games (exchange 7); set wins do not carry over as a quality boost (exchange 5).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Memo - the role of momentum. (1) Momentum is real but bounded. The flow index shows the match state does change: in the final, the index swung from -0.36 (set 1) through +0.16 (set 3) to -0.27 (set 4) to +0.14 (set 5), and each swing was tied to concrete break events. But the swings are not mystical: every one traces to the same mechanism - a player's first-serve percentage dipping, forcing attackable second serves, letting the returner dictate. (2) Runs of points are noise. The longest runs of points in every match are within what pure randomness produces from the same base rates, so a 4- or 5-point run should not change a player's plan; a break, however, changes the state and usually decides the set (hold after a break: 84%; consolidate by holding the next service game). (3) Swings are predictable in location if not in magnitude. The 1.66x lift in the top-risk decile means that when you can see the tell - the opponent missing first serves over the last two games, living on second serves - the break window (2-4 games) is open; outside that window, breaks are at the baseline 16% rate and pressing rarely pays. (4) Preparation and response. Pre-match: build the opponent's serve profile from their recent matches - first-serve rate, second-serve win rate, break-point hold rate; the most vulnerable opponent is the one whose point-winning depends on the serve with no fallback (exchange 9). In-match: after losing a break point, the normal responses are a deliberate serve reset (higher first-serve percentage, safer targets) or a flat, distracted game (exchange 10); the plan should pre-commit to the reset - two or three controlled first serves - because the data shows the vulnerable pattern (another break chance in the same stretch) follows the flat pattern. After winning a break: expect the opponent to hold the next game (84% base rate); the break is only converted into a set when you then hold your own serve, so the consolidation game is as important as the break itself. Do not change form after a set win or loss: the data shows no quality carry-over, and the next set opens at normal hold rates for both players.
